Are the audio "pseudo-genres" real, and does "broader or narrower?" survive a change of definition?

Summary of the three notebooks in RQ4_extension on the Yambda-50M listening logs: a co-listening graph check, a sound-vs-listening comparison (CCA), and a robustness test of the main finding under many definitions of "genre".

1Method flow

Pseudo-genres come from audio; each notebook then tests them against an independent source: how people listen.

Yambda-50M data

29.4M real listens, 9,209 users; organic vs recommended flag; 128-d audio embedding per track, no genre labels
➜

Pseudo-genres

Spherical k-means on audio, k = 8/16/32/64, 3 random starts each. Fitted on 150k tracks, all 848k assigned

302 · Sound vs listening (CCA)

How much of "what is played together" can be predicted from "what it sounds like", and is it just artists or popularity?

Large shared structure

Top canonical correlations 0.90, 0.89, 0.87, 0.83, 0.82; chance ≤ 0.11. Ridge R² = 0.44.

Not artist memorisation

Unseen artists: R² 0.437 vs 0.441 (random tracks); top corr 0.899 vs 0.902.

Not popularity

Leading direction correlates +0.10 with log plays; regressing popularity out leaves R² at 0.434.

Shared axes ≈ pseudo-genre axes

Component 1: 84% (audio) / 70% (listening) of variance lies between the 32 pseudo-genres.

Pseudo-genres are cohesive in listening

Size-weighted lift 0.19 / 0.25 / 0.29 / 0.32 for k = 8–64 vs ~0 shuffled; at k=32 all 32 pseudo-genres are positive.

But not the same partition

Clustering listening gives ARI 0.18–0.34 vs sound (sound vs sound: 0.58–0.74). Read pseudo-genres as a sound-based grouping that listening follows substantially but not fully.

403 · Does the main answer depend on how genre is defined?

Main question: for the same users, is recommended listening broader or narrower than organic? Metric: P(recommended > organic) per user; 0.5 = no difference, below 0.5 = narrower.

DefinitionP(rec > org)Reading
Audio spread (no clustering)0.42narrower
Listening spread (no clustering)0.36narrower
Sound pseudo-genres, hard, k = 8–64 (12 comparisons)0.43–0.46narrower

Listening pseudo-genres, hard, k = 8–64 (12 comparisons)0.41–0.48narrower
Distinct artists (non-sound)0.78broader

Effect size is small

At k=32 the median user has 10 distinct pseudo-genres among 40 organic tracks and 9 among 40 recommended; the direction is consistent across users (recommended lower for 54–63% of users).

Robust to k, method and universe

Hard vs soft, sound vs listening genres, clustering-free measures, three samples: same answer.

6Early versus late: does the variety fade?

Hypothesis: recommended listening starts varied and the recommender then settles on similar sound. We cut the 40 tracks of each stream into windows of 10 and look at variety per window.

Weak support in the streams

Recommended variety falls (audio spread −0.010, pseudo-genres −0.14 from first to last window) while organic rises slightly; the difference in change is −0.018 (−0.024 to −0.012). Only 51–53% of users show a larger decline in recommended.

What drives the narrowing

Recommended listening returns to pseudo-genres it has already played: it adds fewer new ones in every later window. Within any 10 tracks it is not narrower.

Reading

There is a small shift towards a narrower recommended stream as listening goes on, and the recommended share grows by about 3 points inside sessions, but no large fade of sound variety inside a session. Positions in 6.1/6.2 are within a stream, not within a session. Associations only.

Takeaways and open points

Takeaways

  • Pseudo-genres are not just a clustering artefact: visible in the co-listening graph and in listening embeddings, beyond artist and popularity effects.
  • They are a sound-based grouping that listening follows substantially but not fully (ARI 0.18–0.34).
  • Recommended listening is narrower in sound/listening but broader in artists, however genre is defined; the effect is small and grows with the length of the listening stretch (P 0.44 / 0.42 / 0.32 for audio spread at N = 30 / 40 / 100).
  • Early on, recommended listening is slightly broader in sound than organic; later it adds fewer new pseudo-genres, so the variety fades a little. Inside sessions the recommended share rises about 3 points.
  • Recommended streams follow sound more than organic ones (R² 0.64 vs 0.44); cause untested.

Limitations to flag

  • Popular tracks only (≥20 plays; top 10k–40k tracks in the graph).
  • Users with at least 40 distinct tracks per stream only (70% of users; 56% at N = 100). Early-vs-late effects are small and are averages over users.
  • Associations only, one clustering method; no upper reference for modularity; controls cover only recorded artist/album metadata.
  • Linear CCA is a lower bound on shared structure.
